Euler 60

TrianglesGeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: move a triangle until one corner measures 60 degrees and see which line appears.
How to play: Drag a corner, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the centre points, or press a preset button to try a 60-degree triangle.
Look for the math

Something odd happens when a triangle has a 60 degree corner: the line joining its circumcenter and orthocenter cuts the two sides meeting at that corner into an equilateral triangle. Drag the corners to find it, then check the three centre points.

One line, three centres

The centroid, the circumcenter and the orthocenter line up on the Euler line. The applet draws it in red and opens its three little eyes when any angle is 60 degrees, within 0.01 radians. Its checkboxes mark G (centroid), O (circumcenter) and H (orthocenter). If the triangle is equilateral, O and H are the same point, so no line is drawn.

Where the line crosses the sides

Put the 60 degree corner at B, let AB = c and BC = a. A direct calculation from the two centre points gives

BP = BQ = PQ = (a + c) / 3

on the rays BA and BC. Because the angle between those rays is 60 degrees and the two distances from B are equal, triangle PBQ is an equilateral triangle. The line is also perpendicular to the bisector of the 60 degree angle — that is the reformulation on the original page. The logic test checks both facts for 41 different side ratios.

When the condition fits, and a typo

The page says that for such a triangle AP + CQ = PQ is both necessary and sufficient. That holds on the segments exactly when 1/2 ≤ a/c ≤ 2: with t = (a + c)/3 we get AP + CQ = (2c - a + 2a - c)/3 = t = PQ. Press "Long side" to see the other case: one point lands beyond a corner, so the equality fails inside the triangle. Solution 1 on the page prints the slope of AH as 1/√1; its own coordinates give 1/√3, which is what makes AH perpendicular to BC. The live page now embeds a GeoGebra drawing instead of the Java applet (its 2017 Wayback snapshot does too), so the behaviour here comes from the Euler60 bytecode; the claim quoted above is the one printed on the live page. The page credits the problem to Leo Giugiuc, Kadir Altintas and Ruben Dario, and the applet itself to Alexander Bogomolny.

Try the three presets in order: 60° at B, Long side, Equilateral. Tick all three centre boxes and watch where O and H sit each time.
